headline: Manasquan Rocks at First Light: Blues Chop the Surface, Bass Have Gone to Ground
subhead: Six straight days of bluefish limits off Belmar and blitzing surf from Sea Bright to Manasquan — but the stripers want nothing to do with daylight.
body_markdown:
Quarter to six, north side of the Manasquan jetty, and I'm standing next to a kid throwing a Yo-Zuri popper into what looks like a pot of boiling water. Peanut bunker are getting shredded thirty yards off the tip, blues coming up under them like they're being fired out of a cannon, and this kid's grinning like it's his first day on earth. It's not blitz season yet where I need to remind anybody how to act — it's the kind of morning where you just point and cast and something eats.

We flagged this pattern coming — said back on the 24th this was the leading edge of a coastwide blitz, and by the 27th we were calling the bunker-bluefish run the story of the month. Here it is, still running. The boat out of Belmar has strung together six days straight of limit bags, and word from the dock is bigger fish started mixing into those bags around the 27th — proper 6, 7 pound blues, not just the choppers. That's a fresh wave pushing down from the north, and it's been feeding the surf same as it's been feeding the rail.

Water's sitting warm — mid-70s pushing toward 80 in the shallows off the beach — and that's the whole story right there. Blues love it. Bass hate it. Stripers want that 68-to-72 window, and right now the only way to find water that cold on this stretch is to go deep or go dark. I've had two decent nights on the rocks at Sea Bright this week — nothing that'll make the wall at the tackle shop, but a few fish in the 28 to 32 inch range on live eels drifted off the north jetty on the last two hours of the outgoing, into the start of the incoming. That tide change is when the current slows enough for an eel to swim natural instead of getting swept sideways into the rocks. Fished it around 11pm and again just before first light — dead water in between, which tells you these fish are strictly a dark-hours program right now. Bunker chunks on a fishfinder rig, fished tight to the base of the rocks at Manasquan Inlet's south jetty, have taken a couple more after midnight, but you're working for every bite. Anybody telling you the bass bite is easy this week is selling you something.

During the day, forget the stripers and go where the blues are, because that part of the program is honestly fun fishing. Spring Lake and Belmar jetties are holding pods of peanut bunker getting worked over on both tides — I watched three separate blitzes Tuesday morning between 6 and 8am, one right off the Belmar fishing pier, bait getting pushed right up against the rocks and blues crashing through it in full daylight, no subtlety required. Poppers and darters — the old standby Gibbs Polaris, a Super Strike popper if the water's got any chop on it — thrown right into the froth. You don't need finesse. You need to get a lure in the water before the school moves fifty yards down the beach, which they will, over and over, all morning.

Fluke's been the quiet, honest bite while everything else makes noise. We said last week the inlet structure and the nearshore reef sites would carry the fluke program through the full moon tide build, and that's exactly what's happened — steady rather than spectacular, which is about right for this time of year. Manasquan Inlet channel, 20 to 28 feet on the drift, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, working the deeper cuts on the last of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but you're not getting swept into the rocks. Shark River Inlet's been giving up a similar grade of fish — mostly keepers mixed with a lot of shorts, nothing over 4 pounds that I've seen or heard about, but a limit's very doable if you're willing to make three or four drifts through the same stretch. Sea bass are filling out the box on the days the fluke bite is slow to start — same structure, same drift, they just eat first thing before the fluke get moving with the sun higher.

Tide's still carrying some push from the full moon, and that extra flow has helped keep the bait pinned and moving, which is half of why the blitz windows have been so reliable. That's going to ease over the next several days as we drift toward neap, and when it does I'd expect the blitzes to spread out a little — bait less concentrated means the blues have to work harder to find it, and you'll have to work harder to find them. If a thunderstorm rolls through midweek like they tend to in early August, it'll scatter things for a tide or two before it resets.

My plan for the coming week: dawn and last light on the rocks with eels and bunker chunks for stripers, accepting it's a grind; daylight hours chasing the blitz wherever the gulls tell me to go, from Sea Bright down through Spring Lake; and a couple of fluke drifts at Manasquan and Shark River on the tide changes to round out the box. Keep an eye out for the first false albacore scouting reports — too early yet on this stretch, but if that warm-water edge holds and pushes a temperature break up the coast, they won't be far behind the blues.
